title: memory-fragmentation-oom-root-cause-notes-v7
content:
Summary:

These are working notes from the memory fragmentation / OOM investigation (follow-ups from v6). We observed intermittent OOMs on A100-40GB instances when serving long-sequence workloads and under moderate concurrency (4-8 concurrent streams). The goal is to capture evidence, hypotheses, experiments run, and short-term mitigations.

Observed behavior and symptom patterns:
- OOMs are not strictly correlated with peak token throughput; they tend to appear after steady traffic for several minutes.
- Typical failing workload: 8 concurrent requests, avg sequence length 2048 tokens, model = rdlm-13b-quant (HF-flavor quantized to int8 with custom kernels).
- GPUs report ~32–36 GB used at failure on 40 GB A100; reported free memory sometimes shows small-ish free blocks (e.g., 150–600 MB) but total free > 2 GB — implying fragmentation rather than total exhaustion.
- Crash pattern: cudaMalloc returns OOM on allocating a temporary workspace chunk (~200–800 KB to a few MB), despite aggregate free memory sufficient.
- Repro: Increasing request concurrency or sequence length increases frequency. Lowering concurrency to 2-3 reduces failure rate significantly.

Initial instrumentation added (what we measured):
- Hooked allocator stats: allocation count, free block histogram (sizes), total free bytes, largest free block via periodic snapshot.
- NVML sampling every 1s for used/free mem + process-level usage.
- Inserted logging around workspace allocation points (attention workspace, ffn temporary buffers, KV cache resize points).
- Recorded cudaMalloc/cudaFree failure stack traces for first failure.

Key measurements (representative run):
- Before steady state: free=6.1 GB, largest_free_block=5.9 GB
- After ~6 minutes steady traffic: free=2.8 GB, largest_free_block=420 MB, free_blocks_count=482, median_free_block=24 KB
- Fragmentation ratio (1 - largest_free_block / total_free) ~= 0.85 (high)
- Frequent small allocations observed: 8KB–64KB (temp tensors / fused-kernel staging), plus multi-MB allocations for KV growth.

Root-cause hypotheses (ranked):
1) Caching allocator policy + many small ephemeral allocations cause internal fragmentation: allocator holds many small free regions that cannot satisfy larger workspace allocations; our allocator does not coalesce freed blocks aggressively.
2) Mixed allocation sizes across different code paths (KV cache + attention workspaces + per-request scratch) lead to interleaving frees producing fragmentation over time.
3) Use of cudaMalloc/cudaFree for some paths (fallbacks) while other paths use caching allocator prevents reuse of freed memory and leads to externally fragmented GPU heap.
4) Host-to-device pinned staging buffers and cudaHostAlloc fragmentation (less likely, but recorded) also consume addressable device map space on some drivers.

Evidence supporting hypotheses:
- Allocator histograms show a long tail of small free blocks (under 64KB) and a sharp drop in counts for >512KB blocks as time progresses.
- When we forced all allocations to go through the same caching allocator (disabled fallbacks to cudaMalloc path via flag), fragmentation growth slowed substantially and OOMs were not triggered in the same scenario.
- Enabling coalescing in the allocator prototype (experimental) reduced fragmentation ratio from ~0.85 to ~0.32 in a 10-minute run.
- On runs where we triggered KV cache growth (longer sequences), we observed sudden large allocation attempts that failed due to lack of a sufficiently large contiguous block, matching cudaMalloc OOM stack traces.

Experiments performed (details & outcomes):
1) Force single allocator path: route all allocs through caching allocator; outcome: lower failure rate, but small regressions in peak latency due to more metadata bookkeeping.
2) Preallocate large workspace pool at startup (16 GB reserved for temporary workspaces): outcome: no OOMs in tested window, modest improvement in 95p latency; but this reduces headroom for other concurrent workloads and is a blunt instrument.
3) Enable cudaMallocAsync (CUDA 11.2+/driver permitting) for short-lived allocations: outcome: reduced fragmentation for ephemeral allocations; improvement dependent on driver version; not yet universal in infra.
4) Align allocations to 256B or 4KB boundaries and round up small allocations to slab sizes (16KB): outcome: reduced free-block-count and improved coalescing heuristics; lower fragmentation but increased nominal memory usage.
5) KV cache pinning: grow KV cache in large contiguous chunks (power-of-two rounding) instead of many small increments: outcome: fewer large allocations but larger peak usage spikes; tradeoff.

Short-term mitigations (to deploy quickly):
- Config flag to route all small ephemeral allocations through caching allocator and disable direct cudaMalloc fallbacks (feature flag in runtime).
- Limit concurrency per device for long-sequence models (e.g., cap to 4 streams for 13B quantized on A100-40GB) as a conservative safety valve.
- Emergency: configure preallocated workspace pool per model (configurable per-model workspace_size_bytes) — recommended smaller pool (8–12 GB) rather than full reservation.

Mid-term/planned work (engineering backlog):
- Improve allocator coalescing and free-list management (merge adjacent free blocks when possible). Track in INF-3421 (linked).
- Implement slab allocator for small ephemeral tensors (<64KB) to reduce small-block churn.
- Add optional allocator defragmentation routine: pause briefly to migrate live allocations into compacted slabs (risky but possible during low traffic windows / canary rollouts).
- Make KV cache growth strategy pluggable: power-of-two growth vs incremental growth, configurable per model/architecture.
- Evaluate always-on cudaMallocAsync path for ephemeral allocations; requires driver/infra upgrades on some fleets.

Open questions / unresolved items:
- Are there workloads where pre-allocation increases tail latency due to eviction/backpressure? Need wider perf testing.
- Interaction with multi-tenant Dedicated pools: when multiple processes share GPU (MPS or multiple containers), how does inter-process fragmentation behave? Need to capture cross-process free/block visibility.
- Does cuFFT/cuBLAS internal workspace behaviour contribute to fragmentation (they allocate via cudaMalloc internally)? We need to run tests with environment flags to force library workspace reuse.

Repro steps (for engineers):
1) Checkout branch: serving-runtime/investigations/mem-frag-v7 (PR 1284).
2) Start a single A100-40GB instance with driver 525+ and our debug allocator enabled.
3) Run load generator: concurrent_sessions=8, model=rdlm-13b-quant, seq_in=2048 tokens, arrival_rate steady at 1 req/s per session.
4) Capture logs: allocator histograms (every 30s), nvml samples (1s), and record first cudaMalloc OOM stacktrace.
5) Collect snapshots and run analysis script scripts/analyze_mem_frag.py to produce the fragmentation metrics.

Metrics to track in prod dashboards (suggested):
- Fragmentation ratio (1 - largest_free_block / total_free) 1m/5m windows.
- Free blocks count and histogram percentiles (p50, p90 size of free block).
- Time-to-first-oom per hour for model/instance type.
- Correlate allocator churn (allocs/sec) with fragmentation growth.

Action items (who/what/ETA):
- Ben Carter: deploy caching-only allocator flag to canary fleet + monitor (ETA: 2026-03-09).
- Aisha Kapoor: add slab allocator prototype for small buffers and run perf job (ETA: 2026-03-18).
- Lina Gomez: add fragmentation metrics to Prometheus exporter + Grafana dashboard (ETA: 2026-03-12).
- Ravi Menon (owner): coordinate infra driver compatibility checks for cudaMallocAsync and prepare rollout plan (ETA: 2026-03-20).

Notes to reviewers:
- These are iterative investigation notes; experiments changed allocator behavior in ways that affect latency and memory accounting. Please review PR 1284 for code changes and the artifact INF-3421 for the full spec.
- If you have production traces where OOM occurred but allocator snapshots are absent, try to reproduce with the run configuration above and upload logs to the JIRA ticket.

Appendix (quick glossary):
- KV cache: per-request key/value cache used for autoregressive generation. Grows with sequence length.
- Workspace: temporary buffers used by kernels (attention, ffn, fused ops). Often short-lived.
- Caching allocator: allocator that caches cudaMalloc'd blocks to reduce syscall overhead and reuse memory.
- cudaMallocAsync: newer CUDA API that enables asynchronous memory pool allocation with better reuse semantics.

End of notes.
